advisory.title: Multiple timing variability issues in operations intended to be constant-time
advisory.description:
## Summary

Several operations intended to be constant-time could execute secret-dependent
branches, depending on the compiler and target CPU. These include subtraction,
zero counting, division, and Montgomery multiplication.

Additionally, `UintRef` equality could terminate at the first unequal limb,
and `BoxedMontyForm::invert` branched on whether an inverse exists.

## Impact

Applications using affected operations on secret integers may leak information
through timing or microarchitectural side channels. This includes information
about intermediate arithmetic values, matching limbs, and invertibility.

Such leakage could potentially enable recovery of cryptographic secrets.
Practical exploitability depends on the downstream algorithm, compiler, target
CPU, and an attacker's ability to observe the side channel.

## Resolution

Upgrade to v0.7.6, which removes the identified branches, updates `ctutils` to
include its constant-time fixes, and adds BINSEC-based regression checks using
`cargo checkct` for arithmetic on multiple targets.

advisory.title: Non-constant-time mask generation and `u128` comparisons
advisory.description:
## Summary

The `ctutils::Choice` type has mask generation functions for each unsigned
integer size (`u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `u128`). These are `const fn` and
therefore can't reuse the `asm!`-backed mask generation in the `cmov` crate
that's otherwise used to ensure constant-time.

In releases prior to v0.4.4, the generated code from these functions could
include a branch on commonly used platforms. This has been corrected in this
release and now verified on several platforms using BINSEC.

Additionally, `u128` comparison operations provided via `ctutils::Choice` and
intended to work in constant-time were generating branches on 32-bit targets.
This has been resolved via a special case implementation of these functions
for such targets.

## Impact

Branch instructions on secret values can potentially leak such values via
covert channels. This can enable attackers to potentially recover such secrets.

## Resolution

This has been resolved by calling `Choice::to_u8()` when generating the mask,
which in turn uses `black_box` as an optimization barrier. Verification that
this resulted in the desired change in the generated assembly across a variety
of target CPU architectures was performed by BINSEC, which now runs
automatically in CI using `cargo checkct`.

advisory.title: CPU exhaustion during message encoding due to O(n²) name compression
advisory.description:
During message encoding, `hickory-proto`'s `BinEncoder` stores pointers to
labels that are candidates for name compression in a `Vec<(usize, Vec<u8>)>`.
The name compression logic then searches for matches with a linear scan.

A malicious message with many records can both introduce many candidate labels,
and invoke this linear scan many times. This can amplify CPU exhaustion in DoS
attacks.

This is similar to
[CVE-2024-8508](https://www.nlnetlabs.nl/downloads/unbound/CVE-2024-8508.txt).

We recommend all affected users update to `hickory-proto` 0.26.1 for the fix.

advisory.title: NSEC3 closest-encloser proof validation enters unbounded loop on cross-zone responses
advisory.description:
The NSEC3 closest-encloser proof validation in `hickory-proto`'s
`DnssecDnsHandle` walks from the QNAME up to the SOA owner name, building a
list of candidate encloser names. The iterator used assumes the
QNAME is a descendant of the SOA owner, terminating only when the current
candidate equals the SOA name. When the SOA in a response's authority section
is not an ancestor of the QNAME, the loop stalls at the DNS root and never
terminates, repeatedly calling `Name::base_name()` and pushing newly allocated
`Name` and hashed-name entries into the candidate `Vec`.

The bug is reachable by any caller of `DnssecDnsHandle` — including the
resolver, recursor, and client — when built with the `dnssec-ring` or
`dnssec-aws-lc-rs` feature and configured to perform DNSSEC validation. It is
triggered while validating a NoData or NXDomain response whose authority
section contains an SOA record from a zone other than an ancestor of the
QNAME, on a code path that requires NSEC3 closest-encloser proof. In practice
this can be reached through an insecure CNAME chain that crosses zone
boundaries into a DNSSEC-signed zone returning NoData, but the minimum
condition is just a mismatched SOA owner on a response requiring NSEC3
validation.

A `debug_assert_ne!(name, Name::root())` guards the loop body, so debug builds
abort with a panic on the first iteration past the root. Release builds
compile the assertion out and run the loop unbounded, allocating until the
process exhausts available memory (OOM). A reachable upstream attacker who
can return such a response can therefore crash a debug-built validator or
exhaust memory on a release-built one.

The affected code was migrated from `hickory-proto` to `hickory-net` as part of
the 0.26.0 release. The `hickory-proto` 0.26.x release no longer offers
`DnssecDnsHandle` and so we recommend all affected users update to `hickory-net`
0.26.1 when the implementation of that type is required.

advisory.title: Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service
advisory.description:
`NsReader` resolves namespaces by calling `NamespaceResolver::push` for every
`Start`/`Empty` event *before* the event is returned to the caller. `push`
iterated all `xmlns` / `xmlns:*` attributes on the start tag and, for each one,
appended the prefix bytes to an internal buffer and pushed a `NamespaceBinding`
(32 bytes on 64-bit) to an internal `Vec`, with no upper bound on the number of
declarations.

## Impact

A start tag with `N` namespace declarations drove roughly `3×` the tag's byte
size in `NamespaceResolver` heap, allocated *inside* `quick-xml` before the
`NsReader` consumer ever received the event and could inspect or reject it. A
consumer that bounds its *input* size therefore still cannot bound this
allocation: an `M`-byte start tag yields on the order of `3 × M` bytes of
resolver heap the caller never sees.

On untrusted XML this lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker force large heap
allocations with a single start tag. With several `NsReader`s running
concurrently on independent inputs (a common server pattern), the allocations
stack and can exhaust process memory, causing the operating system to kill the
process (OOM). This was confirmed against a real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet
Labs Routinator), where concurrent RRDP validation workers parsing a crafted
`snapshot.xml` exceeded the memory limit and the process was OOM-killed.

## Affected code paths

Consumers using `NsReader` (which always calls `NamespaceResolver::push` before
yielding `Start`/`Empty`), or calling `NamespaceResolver::push` directly. A plain
`Reader` that does not perform namespace resolution is not affected.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`. `NamespaceResolver::push` now rejects a start
tag that declares more than `DEFAULT_MAX_DECLARATIONS_PER_ELEMENT` (256)
namespace bindings, returning the new `NamespaceError::TooManyDeclarations`
instead of allocating without limit. The limit is configurable via
`NamespaceResolver::set_max_declarations_per_element` (use `usize::MAX` to
restore the previous unbounded behavior), and `NsReader::resolver_mut()` is
provided to reach it.

There is no clean workaround for `NsReader` consumers before 0.41.0, as the
allocation happens inside the reader with no configuration knob to cap it.

advisory.title: Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names
advisory.description:
`BytesStart::attributes()` returns an `Attributes` iterator which, by default
(`with_checks(true)`), rejects a start tag that repeats an attribute name. For
each attribute yielded, the iterator compared the new name against every name
seen so far in the same tag using a linear scan, so a start tag with `N`
distinct attribute names cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons. There was no bound on
`N` other than the size of the buffered start tag.

## Impact

Any code that parses untrusted XML and iterates a start tag's attributes with
the default duplicate check enabled can be made to spend CPU time quadratic in
the number of attributes on a single tag. Because the check is pure computation
with no `.await`/I/O, an I/O-based timeout on the consumer (for example a read
or request timeout) cannot interrupt it while it runs.

Measured cost of a single start tag, release build:

| Attributes on one tag | Time |
|---|---|
| 80,000  | ~6 s   |
| 800,000 | ~10 min |

The cost grows with the square of the attribute count, so a start tag of a few
tens of megabytes can stall a parsing thread for hours. No memory is exhausted
and the parser does not crash; the effect is CPU exhaustion on the thread doing
the parsing: a single crafted start tag can pin a CPU core for minutes to hours,
denying service to that worker. A deployment that places a wall-clock bound on
parsing, or confines it to a non-critical thread, may consider the availability
impact lower.

## Affected code paths

* `BytesStart::attributes()` / `Attributes` iterated with checks enabled (the
  default), and `BytesStart::try_get_attribute`.
* `NsReader`, which resolves namespaces by iterating a tag's attributes and so
  reaches the same check internally.

Consumers that iterate attributes with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` and do
not use `NsReader` are not affected.

This was reported as reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker in a
real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet Labs Routinator) via a crafted RRDP
`snapshot.xml`.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`, where the duplicate check keeps the linear
scan for start tags with a small number of attributes and switches to an `O(1)`
hash pre-filter above a threshold, making the whole tag `O(N)`. The reported
`AttrError::Duplicated` positions are unchanged.

If upgrading is not possible and duplicate-name detection is not required,
disable it with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` (this does not help
`NsReader` consumers, which have no equivalent opt-out before 0.41.0).

advisory.title: Zero-length DATAGRAM frames bypass the receive buffer limit in quinn-proto
advisory.description:
quinn-proto bounds its queue of received datagrams by charging each queued frame's payload length
against `TransportConfig::datagram_receive_buffer_size`, evicting the oldest datagrams when the
limit is exceeded. A DATAGRAM frame with an empty payload was charged zero bytes, so it never
triggered eviction and was appended to the queue, which has no other bound.

DATAGRAM frames are not subject to flow control. A peer that has completed the handshake can
therefore send a stream of empty DATAGRAM frames and grow the receiver's heap without limit until
the process is killed. An application that reads incoming datagrams but does so more slowly than
the peer sends them is still affected. Receiving datagrams is enabled by default, so all endpoints
that do not explicitly set `datagram_receive_buffer_size(None)` are affected.

The send path had the same accounting flaw: an application could enqueue an unbounded number of
empty outgoing datagrams without ever receiving `SendDatagramError::Blocked`.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.17 by accounting for the fixed per-datagram overhead in both
directions, so that every queued datagram consumes buffer space.

Thanks to [@alexpyattaev](https://github.com/alexpyattaev) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Unbounded growth of pending connection ID retirements in quinn-proto
advisory.description:
When processing a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame, quinn-proto queues a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame for
each connection ID that the peer asked it to retire. The normal path bounds this queue and closes
the connection with a CONNECTION_ID_LIMIT_ERROR if the bound would be exceeded. However, the path
handling a connection ID that had already been retired pushed onto the queue without applying
the limit and without deduplicating.

A peer that has completed the handshake can first send a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame with a large
`retire_prior_to` value to advance the receiver's connection ID window, and then repeatedly send
NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames with sequence numbers below that window. Each such frame adds another
entry to the queue. The queue is only drained by sending RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames, which are
subject to congestion control, so a peer that withholds acknowledgements can stall the drain while
continuing to flood, growing the victim's memory use without bound.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.17 by applying the same limit on the already-retired path.

Thanks to [@scadastrangelove](https://github.com/scadastrangelove) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Remote peer can panic quinn-proto with zero-length STREAM frames during unordered reads
advisory.description:
When a stream is read in unordered mode (for example through `RecvStream::read(false)` in
quinn-proto or `read_unordered` in `quinn`), quinn-proto proactively deduplicates received data
by recording received ranges in a `RangeSet` through its `replace` method. When an incoming
STREAM frame carried an empty payload, the `Drop` implementation of the iterator returned by
`replace` inserted an empty range into the set, violating the invariant that stored ranges are
non-empty. Subsequent frames overlapping that region then caused a panic while processing the
stream.

A remote peer can trigger this with five small STREAM frames (two of them zero-length) once the
application has put the stream in unordered-read mode. The default ordered read path is not
affected.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by ignoring empty ranges in `RangeSet::replace`.

Thanks to Otto Hermann ([@ojhermann](https://github.com/ojhermann)) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Peer minimum ACK delay can panic quinn-proto when ACK_FREQUENCY transmission is enabled
advisory.description:
When sending ACK_FREQUENCY frames is enabled through
`TransportConfig::ack_frequency_config(Some(..))`, the peer's transport parameters could cause
`AckFrequencyState::candidate_max_ack_delay` to call `Duration::clamp` with a minimum greater
than its maximum, which panics.

For example, a peer advertising a `min_ack_delay` of 100,000 microseconds and a `max_ack_delay`
of 100 milliseconds passes transport parameter validation. At a 5 ms RTT, the lower bound of the
clamp becomes 100 ms while the upper bound is 25 ms, violating the precondition of `clamp` and
panicking while driving the connection. Both automatically derived and explicitly configured
maximum ACK delays use this calculation.

Sending ACK_FREQUENCY frames is disabled by default, so only endpoints that opt in are affected.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by computing the delay with explicit minimum and maximum bounds
instead of `clamp`.

Thanks to [@zerox80](https://github.com/zerox80) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Stream reassembly memory-exhaustion guard in quinn-proto can be bypassed
advisory.description:
The fix for RUSTSEC-2026-0185 in 0.11.15 added a cap on the number of chunks buffered by the
`Assembler` that reassembles out-of-order stream data. However, the cap was only checked inside
the branch that triggers defragmentation, which only runs when the estimated over-allocation
exceeds a threshold proportional to the amount of buffered data. Frames handled entirely by the
unordered-read deduplication loop returned before the check ran at all.

A peer sending one small gapped STREAM frame per packet (for example, 6-byte frames separated by
1-byte gaps) keeps the per-chunk overhead below the defragmentation threshold, so the cap is never
evaluated and the chunk count grows until stream-level flow control stops the peer. With the default
`TransportConfig` (100 concurrent unidirectional streams and a 1.25 MB stream receive window), a
remote, unauthenticated peer can pin roughly 3 GB of receiver memory using about 125 MB of accounted
stream data. The memory is not reclaimed until the affected streams or the connection are closed.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.17 by checking the chunk count after every insert (including in the
unordered deduplication loop) and compacting the buffer once it passes a watermark above the cap.
A stream is rejected once compaction can no longer bring the chunk count back under the cap.

Versions before 0.11.15 are affected by the original, broader issue described in RUSTSEC-2026-0185.

Thanks to Otto Hermann ([@ojhermann](https://github.com/ojhermann)) for reporting and fixing
this issue.

advisory.title: Marvin Attack: potential key recovery through timing sidechannels
advisory.description:
### Impact
Due to a non-constant-time implementation, information about the private key is leaked through timing information which is observable over the network. An attacker may be able to use that information to recover the key.

### Patches
No patch is yet available. The crypto-bigint migration ([RustCrypto/RSA#394](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/pull/394)) did not close this. Tracking is [RustCrypto/RSA#626](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/issues/626) (padding still not constant-time). Implicit rejection work is in [RustCrypto/RSA#680](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/pull/680); default-path blinding is in [RustCrypto/RSA#702](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/pull/702).

Still affected as of 2026-09-12: rsa 0.9.10 (latest stable) and rsa 0.10.0-rc.18 (latest). `patched = []` is intentional.

### Workarounds
Avoid using the `rsa` crate in settings where attackers can observe timing, for example over the network. Local use on a non-compromised computer is fine.

### References
This vulnerability was discovered as part of the "[Marvin Attack]", which revealed several implementations of RSA including OpenSSL had not properly mitigated timing sidechannel attacks.

[Marvin Attack]: https://people.redhat.com/~hkario/marvin/

advisory.title: Certificate verification may accept distrusted intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys when the configured trust anchors allow such paths.
The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

Versions 0.103.16 and 0.104.0-alpha.8 reject paths containing these public keys.

advisory.title: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

Version 0.26.11 is a compatibility wrapper that re-exports
`parent::TLS_SERVER_ROOT_CERTS` from its `webpki-root-certs` 1.x dependency; it
contains no separate root certificate list. Its resolved 1.x dependency must be
updated to 1.0.10 or later.

advisory.title: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

The `webpki-roots` 0.26.11 compatibility package contains no independent trust
store and re-exports the roots from its separately resolved 1.x dependency.
That parent dependency must resolve to 1.0.10 or newer; an older parent remains
affected by this advisory.

advisory.title: Data from an abandoned stream leaks into the next stream on a reused context
advisory.description:
The `with_context` constructors of the stream encoders and decoders used the
borrowed context as it was. When a stream was abandoned on a context, for
example an encoder dropped before `finish()` after an error, whatever it
left there was carried into the next stream: the input buffered by the
previous encoder (up to 128 KiB, or all of it with `zstdmt`) became the
start of the next frame, and a decoder returned undelivered output of the
previous stream.

An application reusing one context for data that must stay separate, such
as different users' requests, could disclose one user's plaintext to
another. Whoever supplies the data can cause the abandonment with invalid
input.

The flaw was corrected by resetting the context's session in
`with_context`.

advisory.title: Uninitialized memory exposed when streaming decompression of a legacy frame fails
advisory.description:
When decompression fails inside a legacy (zstd v0.4 to v0.7) frame, the
bundled zstd library reports the output buffer as fully written although
nothing was written. `DCtx::decompress_stream` committed that position even
on error, and for a `Vec<u8>` destination this extended the vector's length
over uninitialized memory.

Legacy support is enabled by default. A 5- or 6-byte corrupt legacy frame is
enough: through `zstd::stream::write::Decoder`, up to 32 KiB of stale heap
memory is then passed to the wrapped writer on the next `write()` or
`flush()`, or when an `auto_flush()`/`on_flush()` decoder is dropped. Whether
this reaches an attacker depends on where the application sends the
decompressed output. `zstd::stream::read::Decoder`, `zstd::decode_all` and
the bulk API are not affected.

Before zstd-safe 4.0.0, output buffers could only be initialized slices.
The zstd crate's own writer had the same flaw from 0.4.22 to 0.7.x, which is
covered by a separate advisory.

The flaw was corrected by only committing the buffer positions of a
successful call.

advisory.title: `Seekable::decompress` sets a `Vec` length beyond its capacity for offsets past the end
advisory.description:
`ZSTD_seekable_decompress` shortens the requested length to the end of the
data without checking that the offset is before it. For an offset past the
end, it returns a wrapped-around length without writing anything, and
`Seekable::decompress` passed that length to `Vec::set_len`.

With the `seekable` feature, whoever supplies the archive, or chooses the
offset, can leave the caller's `Vec<u8>` with a length far beyond its
capacity. Reading it then discloses neighbouring heap memory, and appending
to it corrupts memory. Offsets near `u64::MAX` can also hang the call.

The flaw was corrected by clamping requests to the end of the data, and by
checking every count reported by the C library against the buffer capacity.

advisory.title: WebAssembly allocator shim corrupts memory on allocation failure
advisory.description:
On wasm32, zstd-sys provides `malloc` and `free` to the C library through a
shim over Rust's allocator. The shim did not check for allocation failure:
it wrote its size header to address 0 and returned address 4, which the C
library used as a valid buffer. `free(NULL)` also read below address 0.

Whenever the instance cannot grow its memory by what a frame asks for, a
small crafted frame (a 9-byte header declaring a 128 MiB window is enough)
made decompression write decoded data over the bottom of the module's
linear memory, instead of failing. The corruption stays within the wasm
sandbox.

The flaw was corrected by returning NULL on allocation failure or size
overflow, and by making `free(NULL)` a no-op.

advisory.title: unsafe-libyaml is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The [repository](https://github.com/dtolnay/unsafe-libyaml) was archived by
its owner on 2024-03-25 and is read-only. The last release is 0.2.11
(March 2024).

`unsafe-libyaml` is a machine translation of libyaml's C code into unsafe
Rust (c2rust). Bugs found in it will not be fixed upstream. It is used by
`serde_yaml` (itself deprecated) and by forks such as `serde_yaml_ng`.

## Alternatives

Consider a YAML parser written in safe Rust, for example:

- [saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/saphyr) ([serde-saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/serde-saphyr) for serde users)
- [noyalib](https://crates.io/crates/noyalib)

advisory.title: `zbus_names` is unmaintained
advisory.description:

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `names` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus name types.

advisory.title: `zvariant` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zvariant` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `wire` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format. Users of the GVariant format should migrate to [`zgvariant`](https://crates.io/crates/zgvariant).

advisory.title: `zvariant_derive` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zvariant_derive` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

Its derive macros are provided by [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format.

advisory.title: Unsoundness in `Error::downcast_mut()`
`event-listener` allows `!Send` tags to cross thread boundaries via `StackSlot`
advisory.description:
Affected versions of `event-listener` unconditionally implement `Send` and
`Sync` for `StackSlot<'_, T>`, the stack-allocated listener type created
by the `listener!` macro.

This allows a `!Send` tag type set via `Event::with_tag` to be moved to
another thread and accessed via `StackSlot::wait`, causing a data race in safe
code.

advisory.title: Potential use-after-free due to lack of panic safety in `LruCache::pop()`
advisory.description:
`LruCache::pop()` in `lru` was not panic-safe. If the `Drop` implementation of a stored key panics during `pop()`, `self.detach()` is never called, leaving dangling pointers in the internal doubly-linked list.

A subsequent cache operation that triggers eviction can then dereference these dangling pointers:
- The node is freed from the map, but remains linked in the LRU list due to the skipped `detach()` call
- When a new insertion causes eviction, the LRU traversal encounters the dangling pointer
- This results in a write to already-freed memory during the eviction process

## Impact

- **CWE-416 (Use-After-Free):** memory corruption when subsequent cache operations access freed node pointers in the linked list
- **CWE-415 (Double Free):** potential heap corruption when the same memory is freed multiple times

Both types of undefined behavior can be invoked in safe Rust, but only if unwinding panics are enabled and `std::panic::catch_unwind` is used with key types that have potentially-panicking `Drop` implementations.

## Fix

Fixed in `lru` 0.18.2 by detaching the node from the linked list before freeing it and dropping the key ([lru-rs#238](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/pull/238)).

advisory.title: `IterMut` violates Stacked Borrows by invalidating internal pointer
advisory.description:
Affected versions of this crate contain a soundness issue in the `IterMut`
iterator implementation. The `IterMut::next` and `IterMut::next_back`
methods temporarily create an exclusive reference to the key when
dereferencing the internal node pointer.

This invalidates the shared pointer held by the internal `HashMap`,
violating Stacked Borrows rules.

advisory.title: Rand is unsound with a custom logger using `rand::rng()`
advisory.description:
It has been reported (by [@lopopolo](https://github.com/lopopolo)) that the `rand` library is [unsound](https://rust-lang.github.io/unsafe-code-guidelines/glossary.html#soundness-of-code--of-a-library) (i.e. that safe code using the public API can cause Undefined Behaviour) when all the following conditions are met:

- The `log` and `thread_rng` features are enabled
- A [custom logger](https://docs.rs/log/latest/log/#implementing-a-logger) is defined
- The custom logger accesses `rand::rng()` (previously `rand::thread_rng()`) and calls any `TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods on `ThreadRng`
- The `ThreadRng` (attempts to) reseed while called from the custom logger (this happens every 64 kB of generated data)
- Trace-level logging is enabled or warn-level logging is enabled and the random source (the `getrandom` crate) is unable to provide a new seed

`TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods for `ThreadRng` use `unsafe` code to cast `*mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>` to `&mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>`. When all the above conditions are met this results in an aliased mutable reference, violating the Stacked Borrows rules. Miri is able to detect this violation in sample code. Since construction of [aliased mutable references is Undefined Behaviour](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/nomicon/references.html), the behaviour of optimized builds is hard to predict.

advisory.title: `AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate I/O safety
advisory.description:
`tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd` provides safe constructors (`new`, `with_interest`, `try_new`, and `try_with_interest`) that accept any `T: AsRawFd` rather than requiring proof of ownership or validity of the file descriptor. Because `RawFd` implements `AsRawFd`, safe code can construct an `AsyncFd` from an arbitrary or closed file descriptor, or close/replace the underlying file descriptor while the `AsyncFd` is still alive.

This violates I/O safety in two ways:

1. `AsyncFd<T>` implements `AsFd` for all `T: AsRawFd` by calling `BorrowedFd::borrow_raw(self.as_raw_fd())`, allowing safe code to obtain an arbitrary `BorrowedFd<'_>` without owning the file descriptor.
2. Tokio's I/O driver stores a pointer to an internal allocation in the `epoll`/`kqueue` user data for registered file descriptors. If the underlying file descriptor is duplicated and then closed while an `AsyncFd` is alive, and the OS reuses that file descriptor number for a another IO resource on the same runtime, dropping the first `AsyncFd` deregisters the reused file descriptor number and frees the first while the original file description remains registered in `epoll`, leading to a use-after-free when a readiness event fires.

Starting in Tokio 1.51.6, 1.53.3, and 1.54.0, `AsyncFd::new`, `AsyncFd::with_interest`, `AsyncFd::try_new`, and `AsyncFd::try_with_interest` are deprecated in favor of the `unsafe` constructors `AsyncFd::register` and `AsyncFd::register_with_interest`. Callers must ensure that the file descriptor remains valid, open, and unchanged for the lifetime of the `AsyncFd`.

advisory.title: Use-after-free with `CParameter::StableInBuffer`
advisory.description:
With `CParameter::StableInBuffer(true)` (`experimental` feature), the C
library keeps a pointer to the input of one streaming call and reads from it
in later calls, including `flush_stream` and `end_stream`, which take no
input. An `InBuffer` only borrows its slice for one call, so safe code could
free it in between, and freed memory was compressed into the frame. The C
library behaves this way since zstd 1.5.4, whether bundled or linked from the
system.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to enable the parameter.

advisory.title: Heap buffer overflow in `CCtx::try_clone` on a multithreaded context
advisory.description:
`CCtx::try_clone` (`experimental` feature, deprecated) copies tables sized
from the context's applied parameters. Starting a multithreaded frame
(`zstdmt` feature) replaces those parameters with the workers' without
resizing the context's own tables, so after an abandoned single-threaded
frame, the copy wrote up to 512 KiB past a heap allocation, or read past
one. This became reachable with the bundled zstd 1.5.6.

The flaw was corrected by refusing `try_clone` (and the unsafe
`compress_block`) once `NbWorkers` was set on the context.

advisory.title: Use-after-free when changing a multithreaded context with an unfinished frame
advisory.description:
When a multithreaded frame (`zstdmt` feature, `CParameter::NbWorkers`) is
left unfinished, its jobs may still be running on the worker threads: the C
library only waits for them when the next frame starts, or when the context
is freed. A session reset makes the context accept changes again in the
meantime, so:

- unloading the dictionary (`load_dictionary`, `ref_cdict`, `ref_prefix`,
  `disable_dictionary`, `init*`, or `reset` with parameters) freed the
  dictionary a worker was still compressing against;
- changing `NbWorkers` made the next frame resize the job table before
  waiting for the old jobs.

The flaw was corrected by refusing these calls while a multithreaded frame
is unfinished. The new `CCtx::wait_for_workers()` waits for the workers
first.

advisory.title: Double free in `DCtx::try_clone`
advisory.description:
`DCtx::try_clone` (`experimental` feature, deprecated) is a plain copy of the
C context. A context owning a dictionary (from `load_dictionary`,
`ref_prefix` or `init_using_dict`) or a dictionary table (`ref_ddict` with
`RefMultipleDDicts`) ended up with both copies freeing it. A context cloned
mid-frame resumed on uninitialized stream state. The clone also silently lost
the `WindowLogMax` limit.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to clone such contexts, and by carrying
over the parameters the copy leaves out.

advisory.title: Use-after-free of a dictionary after a one-shot call on a context with an open stream
advisory.description:
The one-shot `DCtx` and `CCtx` methods assumed the C library resets the
context, but it leaves an open stream as it is. When a stream was left
unfinished on a context, a one-shot call such as `decompress_using_dict`
could leave the context pointing at the dictionary borrowed for that call,
and the next streaming call resumed the stream against it after it was
freed: decompressed output then contained freed heap memory. On the
compression side, the stream resumed against the one-shot call's buffers.

This requires an application to use one context for both streaming and
one-shot calls without a reset in between. The flaw was corrected by
resetting the session after one-shot calls whenever a stream may be open.

advisory.title: Use-after-free through `init_using_cdict` and `init_using_ddict`
advisory.description:
`CCtx::init_using_cdict` and `DCtx::init_using_ddict` (`experimental`
feature, deprecated) took the dictionary as `&CDict<'b>` and `&DDict<'b>`
with only `'b: 'a`, so the dictionary itself could be dropped while the
context still pointed at it. The same mistake in other constructors was
fixed earlier (<https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/issues/365>).

The flaw was corrected by taking `&'a CDict<'b>` and `&'a DDict<'b>`.

advisory.title: Out-of-bounds read in `train_from_buffer` when sample sizes overflow
advisory.description:
`ZDICT_trainFromBuffer` is never told the length of the samples buffer, so
`train_from_buffer` checked that the sample sizes add up to it. With
overflow checks off, as in release builds, that sum wrapped around: sizes
totalling 2^64 plus the buffer length passed the check, and the trainer read
past the end of the buffer. `zstd::dict::from_continuous` relies on this
check from zstd 0.4.10; older versions of zstd had their own, covered by a
separate advisory.

This requires the sample sizes to come from an untrusted source. The flaw
was corrected by summing the sizes with overflow checks.

advisory.title: Out-of-bounds read with an out-of-range `InBuffer::pos`
advisory.description:
`InBuffer`'s fields are public, so safe code can set `pos` past the end of
`src`. The position was passed to the C library unchecked, and
`ZSTD_seekable_compressStream`, unlike the other streaming functions, does
not validate it: it read past the end of the input slice, by up to the
frame size, and compressed that memory into the output.

The flaw was corrected by checking the position before every call into the
C library.

advisory.title: `OutBuffer::around_pos` exposes uninitialized memory
advisory.description:
`OutBuffer::around_pos` accepted a position past the initialized length of a
`Vec<u8>`. The next streaming call then marked everything before the
position as initialized, so safe code could read stale heap memory between
the vector's previous length and that position.

The flaw was corrected by zero-filling that gap.

advisory.title: `Seekable` reads a NULL or out-of-bounds seek table
advisory.description:
`Seekable` did not record whether it was initialized. On a fresh `Seekable`,
or one whose `init_buff()` failed, `decompress`, `offset_to_frame_index` and
`frame_decompressed_size` made the C library read a NULL seek table. After a
failed re-initialization, `decompress` returned data from the refused buffer
using the previous seek table.

Separately, `frame_decompressed_size(num_frames())`, on `Seekable` and
`SeekTable`, read one entry past the end of the seek table.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to use a `Seekable` until an
initialization succeeded, and by checking the frame index.
